reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID (Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease)
clinicalPearls: Type I results from deficiency of proline oxidase (proline dehydrogenase, PRODH) and is usually a benign biochemical finding, with only modest elevation of plasma proline
Type II results from deficiency of pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C) dehydrogenase and produces higher plasma proline together with accumulation of P5C in blood and urine
The distinctive marker of type II is raised delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate, which can be sought biochemically to separate the two forms
Type II is more consistently associated with seizures, sometimes provoked by febrile illness, and P5C is thought to inhibit vitamin B6-dependent enzymes by inactivating pyridoxal phosphate
The chromosome 22q11 region containing PRODH means proline elevation may be seen in association with the 22q11 deletion phenotype
Neither type has a firmly established disease-modifying therapy; type II seizures are managed symptomatically and vitamin B6 status merits attention
Both are autosomal recessive, and the biochemical elevation of proline can be an incidental screening finding
British-spelling amino acid nomenclature (proline, hyperprolinaemia) applies throughout
reference.pathophysiology: Proline is catabolised in two sequential mitochondrial steps: proline oxidase converts proline to delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C), and P5C dehydrogenase then oxidises P5C to glutamate. Type I hyperprolinaemia reflects loss of proline oxidase, causing a relatively mild rise in plasma proline that is often clinically silent. Type II reflects loss of P5C dehydrogenase, so both proline and its upstream intermediate P5C accumulate; the reactive P5C can bind and inactivate pyridoxal-5-phosphate, impairing vitamin B6-dependent reactions and contributing to a lowered seizure threshold. The disorders are distinguished biochemically by the presence of elevated P5C in type II.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary hyperprolinaemia from lactic acidosis or hyperlactataemia (proline oxidase is redox-sensitive)
Other benign aminoacidaemias detected on newborn or metabolic screening
Renal tubular disease causing generalised aminoaciduria
Malnutrition or hepatic dysfunction altering plasma amino acids
additionalInvestigations: Quantitative plasma amino acids to grade the degree of proline elevation
Assay for delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate to identify type II
Urine amino and organic acid analysis
Molecular testing of PRODH (type I) and ALDH4A1 (type II)
Plasma lactate to exclude secondary elevation of proline
EEG and vitamin B6 status evaluation when seizures occur
redFlags: Seizures, particularly febrile or difficult-to-control episodes, in the type II phenotype
Coexisting features suggesting a 22q11 deletion syndrome
Marked proline elevation with acidosis suggesting a secondary or additional metabolic problem
reference.prognosis: Type I is generally benign with a normal outlook. Type II may be associated with seizures and variable neurodevelopmental outcome, though many affected individuals do well, and management is largely supportive.
pitfalls: Failing to distinguish types I and II, and thereby overlooking the seizure risk of type II
Ignoring secondary causes of raised proline such as lactic acidosis
Attributing all neurological features to the biochemical abnormality without wider evaluation
references: Scriver's OMMBID: disorders of proline and hydroxyproline metabolism
Nyhan, Atlas of Inherited Metabolic Diseases
management: No disease-modifying drug therapy; type I is generally benign and managed with reassurance
Anticonvulsant therapy for the seizures more consistently associated with type II, especially when febrile-illness provoked
Attention to vitamin B6 status with pyridoxine supplementation, given P5C-mediated inactivation of pyridoxal phosphate in type II
Antipyretic measures during febrile illness to lower seizure risk
Consider evaluation for a 22q11 deletion given the PRODH gene location, with associated developmental support where relevant
Genetic counselling and family screening, distinguishing type I from type II biochemically
